title: Weapons Not of the World: Paul Answers His Critics
summary: Paul turns sharply to confront those in Corinth who say he is bold in letters but weak in person. He insists that he does not fight with worldly weapons but with divine power that demolishes strongholds and takes every thought captive to obey Christ. He refuses to measure himself by others' standards or boast in work others have done, and he boasts only within the field God assigned him, since it is the Lord's commendation, not self-commendation, that counts.
story: Chapters 1-9 ended in warmth and confidence. Chapter 10 opens a new section (chapters 10-13) with a very different tone: defensive, ironic, and at times severe. Paul now addresses directly the rivals he has hinted at earlier (2:17; 3:1; 5:12), whom he will call false apostles and "super-apostles" in chapter 11, and the members of the church who have been influenced by them. This chapter sets out the terms of the dispute: what makes someone a true servant of Christ, and by what standard he should be judged.
historical:
The sudden change in tone at chapter 10 is one of the main reasons many scholars think 2 Corinthians combines more than one letter. Some identify chapters 10-13 with the tearful letter mentioned in 2:4 and 7:8, written before chapters 1-9; others think chapters 10-13 were written after chapters 1-9, when Paul received fresh news that the situation had worsened. Still others defend the unity of the letter, suggesting Paul turns deliberately to the unresolved problem of the rival teachers after first securing his relationship with the majority, or that he wrote over a period of time. The manuscripts give no sign of a break.

The rivals themselves appear to have been Jewish Christian missionaries (11:22) who arrived in Corinth with letters of recommendation, claimed special status as apostles, accepted financial support, and presented themselves impressively. They criticized Paul's unimpressive presence and speech (verse 10) and perhaps his refusal to accept payment (11:7). Whether they taught the same law-observant message as the agitators in Galatia is debated; they seem more concerned with status, eloquence, and spiritual experiences than with circumcision.
cultural:
In the Greek cities, public speaking was an art and a form of entertainment, and a speaker's physical presence, voice, and delivery were judged as closely as his arguments. Rhetorical education trained men to impress audiences, and professional orators could become celebrities. Paul's critics said, "His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account" (verse 10). By the standards of Corinthian culture, that was a serious charge.

Paul's military imagery in verses 3-6 would have been vivid in a Roman colony. Siege warfare involved demolishing fortifications and towers, and captives were led away after a city fell. Paul applies the picture to arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God. The word kanon in verses 13-15, translated "limits" and "field of influence", meant a measuring rod or a defined area; in Roman administration it could describe an assigned territory. Paul claims that God assigned him a field that included Corinth, since he was the first to bring the gospel there.
literary: The chapter is framed by irony. It opens with Paul quoting his critics' description of him, "humble when face to face with you, but bold when away" (verse 1), and it closes with a quotation from Jeremiah 9:24 that Paul also used in 1 Corinthians 1:31: "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." Between these come the military metaphor (verses 3-6), a response to the charge of inconsistency (verses 7-11), and a critique of self-measurement (verses 12-18), where the repetition of "themselves" in verse 12 mocks those who compare themselves only with themselves. The word "boast" and its relatives become frequent from here to the end of chapter 12, as Paul reluctantly adopts his opponents' method in order to expose it.

outline.t: The same in letters and in person
Boasting within the field God assigned
Boast in the Lord; his commendation counts

doctrines.note: The conflict Paul describes is real but not fought with the world's weapons. Its targets are arguments, pretensions, and thoughts set against the knowledge of God, and its aim is obedience to Christ. The kingdom advances by truth and divine power, not by coercion or impressive self-presentation.

Paul's authority was given "for building you up rather than tearing you down" (verse 8). Leadership in the church exists to build up the community, and it is judged by that purpose, not by status, eloquence, or comparison with rivals.
Paul exposes the habit of measuring ourselves by comparison with others. Only the Lord's commendation matters (verse 18). Human worth and ministry are defined by God's calling, not by self-promotion.

words.note: Epieikeia, gentleness, reasonableness, forbearance, a willingness to yield rather than insist on one's rights. Paul appeals "by the mildness and gentleness of Christ" (verse 1). He begins his most combative section by invoking Christ's gentleness, which he means to reflect even while he confronts.

Ochyroma, stronghold, fortress. It appears only here in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it describes fortified cities. Paul's strongholds are not demons or places but arguments and proud reasoning raised against the knowledge of God.

Aichmalotizo, to take captive, literally to capture by the spear. Paul pictures every thought as a prisoner of war brought into obedience to Christ. The image is of a mind whose loyalties are reordered, not of a mind shut down.

Kauchaomai, to boast, to take pride in. The verb and its related nouns appear more often in 2 Corinthians than in any other New Testament book. Boasting can be sinful self-exaltation or proper confidence; Paul's rule is Jeremiah's, to boast only in the Lord.

christ: Paul's appeal begins with "the mildness and gentleness of Christ" (verse 1). Jesus described himself as gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29), and Paul presents that gentleness as the pattern for his own conduct, even as he warns of discipline. The goal of every argument is "to make it obedient to Christ" (verse 5): the aim is not to win debates but to bring people and their thinking under the lordship of Christ. Paul belongs to Christ (verse 7), carries the gospel of Christ (verse 14), and seeks only the Lord's commendation (verse 18). The authority he exercises is Christ's, given for building up.
questions: Paul's critics judged him by his presence and speaking ability. What standards do churches today use to judge leaders, and how do they compare with Paul's?
What would it mean in practice to take every thought captive to obey Christ in an area where your thinking is currently undisciplined?
Verse 12 warns against measuring ourselves by comparison with others. Where does comparison most distort how you see yourself or your work?
